newsitem.title: UK: Former British minister denies fresh sleaze claims.
newsitem.headline: Former British minister denies fresh sleaze claims.

text.p: A former Conservative minister on Tuesday angrily denied fresh newspaper claims that he accepted cash for asking parliamentary questions and vowed on Tuesday that he would clear his name.
Neil Hamilton stopped a case against the Guardian newspaper that was billed as the libel trial of the century only hours before it had been due to start on Tuesday.
He insisted that he had dropped the case only because he could not afford the legal fees. Parliamentary lobbyist Ian Greer simultaneously dropped his libel case against the Guardian.

"They're doing a hatchet job on me," Hamilton told BBC Radio. "They have never been printed by the newspaper before, and why? Because they thought I had the resources to sue them. Yesterday they discovered I had run out of money. Today they print them. I think that speaks for itself."
The Guardian said its evidence to the court would have revealed "a pattern of parliamentary sleaze more far reaching than anyone had imagined".

Hamilton was forced to resign as trade minister in October 1994 after the Guardian accused him of accepting money from Mohammed al-Fayed, the Egyptian-born owner of London's luxury Harrods store, in return for tabling questions in parliament.
Tuesday's Guardian report revived a controversy over sleazy behaviour within the Conservatives that has resulted in the resignation of 16 of its MPs from government posts since 1992.

The Guardian named four other senior Conservatives who it said were involved in a paid campaign to promote the interests of the Harrods boss. It based its claims on government documents released for the trial and witness statements.
It said that if the libel case had gone ahead "a nauseating portrait would have emerged of of MPs on the take".

Prime Minister John Major and deputy premier Michael Heseltine had been subpoenaed to give evidence in what threatened to be an explosive case on the eve of the ruling party's last political conference before an election.
In a statement on Monday, the Guardian said the decision not to proceed "must be one of the most astonishing legal cave-ins in the history of the law of libel".
Hamilton said he would continue to fight the allegations by other means and would ask the parliamentary commissioner for standards to investigate.

Judge Lord Michael Nolan, who chaired a commission into standards in public life called by Major to limit the political damage of the sleaze allegations, called for the matter to be "investigated without delay".
"The continuing accusations and counter accusations in this case are damaging to the reputation of parliament, and the truth of the matter needs to be properly investigated," he said.

Guardian editor Alan Rusbridger claimed Hamilton had backed out because he knew he could not win. Hamilton's decision followed the release to both sides in the libel case of what the Guardian called crucial government documents.
It alleged that Hamilton persistently asked for money from al-Fayed and would visit his office to collect payment.
